overview: The Han ruled China for four centuries, with a brief interruption, and set the pattern that later dynasties followed: an emperor advised by scholar-officials trained in the Confucian classics, a census-taking bureaucracy, and a capital laid out on a grid. Paper, the seismoscope and the first great history of China were made under the Han, and the Silk Road opened during their reign. The Chinese still call their majority people the Han.

items.text: Cai Lun presents the court with paper made from bark, hemp and rags. Paper travels west along the Silk Road and reaches Europe a thousand years later.
Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope: a bronze vessel that dropped a ball into one of eight dragon mouths to show the direction of a distant earthquake.
The wheelbarrow, the crank handle and the stern-mounted rudder are all first attested in Han China.
The Taichu calendar reform sets the civil year, with its intercalary months, on the footing that Chinese calendars follow in principle to this day.
The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: systems of linear equations solved by a method equivalent to Gaussian elimination, rules for negative numbers, and an approximation of pi.
Zhang Heng's water-driven armillary sphere turns with the heavens, and he catalogues about 2,500 stars.
Xu Shen's Shuowen Jiezi, the first dictionary to analyse Chinese characters by their components, is presented to the throne.
Du Shi harnesses a water wheel to the bellows of a blast furnace. Cast iron becomes cheap enough for ploughshares and hoes.
Brine wells drilled hundreds of meters deep with bamboo derricks in Sichuan, and natural gas piped through bamboo to boil the brine for salt.
Silk woven on multi-shaft treadle looms. Han silks have been found in Roman-era graves at Palmyra in Syria.
The tombs at Mawangdui are sealed, preserving silk paintings, a silk map, and the earliest complete copies of the Daodejing.
Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, 130 chapters covering two thousand years and the model for every later Chinese dynastic history.
The fu rhapsodies of Sima Xiangru, the folk songs collected by the Music Bureau, and lacquerware from Sichuan workshops exported across Asia.
Emperor Wu makes the Confucian classics the basis of official learning; the Imperial Academy follows in 124 BCE.
The White Horse Temple at Luoyang, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, marks the arrival of Buddhism along the Silk Road.
Wang Chong's Lunheng argues that thunder is not the anger of heaven and that the dead have no consciousness.
Zhang Daoling founds the Way of the Celestial Masters in Sichuan, the first organized Daoist religion.
Zhang Qian sets out for the west. His reports of Ferghana horses, Parthia and India open what is now called the Silk Road.
The Protectorate of the Western Regions is set up in the Tarim Basin, securing the route to Central Asia.
An embassy claiming to come from the Roman emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court by sea, according to the Book of Later Han.
The census counts 57,671,400 people, most of them farming households of about five on small plots of millet, wheat and rice, taxed in grain, cloth and labour.
Chang'an, the Western Han capital, sits inside about 25 km of walls with nine markets, and is one of the two largest cities in the world alongside Rome.
Games of liubo and cuju kickball, and the clay tomb figures of dancers, farmyards and watchtowers that show the Han world in miniature.

fall.text: Weakened by court factions and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184, the dynasty ended when Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian in 220. China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.

sources.title: Michael Loewe, Everyday Life in Early Imperial China (1968)
The Cambridge History of China, volume 1: The Ch'in and Han Empires (1986)
